sources.name: Ars Technica
sources.title: Amazon says hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input

stories.headline: Amazon says attackers' AI agents found and exploited a zero-day alone
stories.dek: Agents running on the open source Cairn pentesting framework took a one-line goal and gained full control of a university server, Amazon says.
stories.body:
Amazon says attackers used AI agents to find and exploit a previously unknown vulnerability with almost no human involvement, Ars Technica reports. The only human input was a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server.

The agents ran on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. According to Amazon, the attackers wrote their prompts in simplified Chinese and set the model to the China Standard Time zone. They gave the agents a list of IP addresses and one goal: "obtain shell access." The agents quickly found a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers, exploited it, and took full control of the system.

"These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable," Amazon said.

Cairn was built for defenders. It is an open source problem-solving engine, and autonomous penetration testing is its first validated domain. Users supply a goal and optional hints. A server keeps a shared graph of facts and hints, and a dispatcher reads that graph, schedules tasks and hands each project to a dedicated worker container running several agents at once. The framework is model-agnostic and works with back ends including Claude Code, Codex and Pi. Researchers at Palo Alto Networks have also seen it used with GLM 5.2, DeepSeek V4 Flash and DeepSeek V4 Pro.

Amazon's report is not the first sign of attackers using Cairn. Earlier this month, Palo Alto Networks said hackers used the framework against organizations in the semiconductor, defense and civil society sectors. That campaign ran 25 autonomous operations against at least 19 organizations and breached at least 10 of them.

Amazon did not name the university or the vulnerable medical imaging application in the details Ars Technica reported. It is also unclear whether the university incident is linked to the campaign Palo Alto Networks described.
key_points: Amazon says Cairn-based AI agents found and exploited a zero-day autonomously
Target was an open source medical imaging AI app on a university server
Palo Alto Networks tied Cairn to 25 operations against 19+ organizations
At least 10 organizations breached in that earlier campaign
stories.why_it_matters: Open source agent tooling built for pentesters is now finding real zero-days for attackers, which shortens the window between deploying an exposed service and getting owned. Anyone self-hosting open source AI apps should assume automated agents will probe them.

sources.title: VMware vCenter Hit by Another Critical 9.8-Rated Auth Bypass Flaw After Zero-Day Exploitation

stories.headline: Broadcom patches 23 VMware flaws, including critical vCenter auth bypass
stories.dek: The 9.8-rated vCenter bug arrives days after a separate directory service flaw was exploited as a zero-day by suspected Chinese spies.
stories.body:
Broadcom has released patches for 23 vulnerabilities across VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion and Avi Load Balancer, The Hacker News reports. The most serious, CVE-2026-123903, is an authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service (vmdir) rated 9.8 out of 10 on CVSS. "A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system," Broadcom said.

vCenter also gets fixes for four high-severity bugs rated 7.5: an archive-processing file write flaw that could lead to code execution, and three denial-of-service issues in vmdir. Fixes ship in vCenter 8.0 U3m and in Cloud Foundation releases 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300 and 5.2.5.

The update follows a patch days earlier for CVE-2026-123890, a separate vmdir auth bypass exploited by a suspected China-nexus group called Armory Castle. Broadcom says the new bugs are unrelated and has not reported them exploited.
key_points: CVE-2026-123903 is a 9.8-rated vCenter authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service.
Broadcom fixed 23 flaws across ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion and Avi Load Balancer.
A separate vmdir bypass, CVE-2026-123890, was recently exploited as a zero-day by suspected China-nexus group Armory Castle.

sources.title: New Shirudo tool uses AI to shield unpatched Linux systems from exploits

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: OpenAI and Cisco Unveil AI-Assisted Linux Security Tool to Block Exploits Before Patching

stories.headline: OpenAI and Cisco release Shirudo to shield unpatched Linux systems
stories.dek: The open-source runtime lets AI agents write eBPF "shields" that block exploits without restarts, with deployment kept under human control.
stories.body:
OpenAI and Cisco have released Shirudo, an open-source Linux runtime that lets AI agents deploy temporary protections against exploits while admins prepare and roll out patches. The tool uses eBPF to block vulnerable code paths without restarting services. In a test, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit against a running Elasticsearch service, OpenAI said.

Shirudo is a rewrite of Tetragon, the eBPF security platform from Cisco-owned Isovalent. Agents reproduce an exploit, write a targeted shield and validate it, and an operator approves enforcement. Shields ship as signed .bee packages via an OCI registry and are verified with TPMs. They retire when the real patch lands.

Not everyone is convinced. Expel researcher Marcus Hutchins told BleepingComputer that letting AI agents write rules affecting the kernel may not be a good idea.
key_points: Shirudo is open source (BSD + GPL), Linux-only and built on Isovalent's Tetragon.
Shields are signed .bee packages verified with TPMs; operators approve before blocking.
OpenAI will hold a technical webinar on the tool on December 15.

sources.name: Hacker News
sources.title: Matrix Multiplication is Θ(n^2.25) [pdf]

stories.headline: Preprint claims matrix multiplication exponent is exactly 2.25
stories.dek: A PDF in an OpenAI GitHub repository asserts a tight Θ(n^2.25) bound, an unverified claim that would be a major complexity result.
stories.body:
A preprint claiming that matrix multiplication takes Θ(n^2.25) time topped Hacker News on Wednesday, drawing 398 points and 196 comments. The paper, titled "The matrix multiplication exponent is nine fourths" and dated November 24, 2026, is hosted as a PDF in the openai/math repository on GitHub.

The claim has not been verified. The Θ notation means the paper asserts both an upper and a lower bound: that n-by-n matrices can be multiplied in roughly n^2.25 operations, and that no algorithm can do fundamentally better. That would pin the exponent to exactly nine fourths.

If it holds up, the result would settle one of the central open questions in algorithmic complexity theory. Matrix multiplication underpins much of scientific computing and machine learning. Extraordinary claims of this kind typically face months of scrutiny before experts accept them.
key_points: A preprint titled "The matrix multiplication exponent is nine fourths," dated November 24, 2026, is hosted in the openai/math GitHub repository.
It claims a tight Θ(n^2.25) bound for matrix multiplication, a result that remains unverified.
The paper topped Hacker News with 398 points and 196 comments.

sources.title: Tidal to Ban Fully AI-Generated Music, Remove Millions of Existing Tracks

stories.headline: Tidal bans fully AI-generated music, will delete 27 million tracks
stories.dek: The streamer says 60 percent of new uploads on November 6 were entirely AI-made, and it will purge them on December 9.
stories.body:
Tidal will ban music created entirely by AI and delete the 27 million AI-labeled tracks on its service on December 9, Ars Technica reports. Those tracks make up 6.3 percent of Tidal's catalog. The company says the move will have almost no impact on listening, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days.

Tidal introduced an AI policy in July 2026 that labeled and demonetized fully AI-generated songs. It did not slow the flood. Tidal says 43 percent of new uploads over the past 90 days were completely AI-generated, rising to 60 percent on November 6.

The company cites harm to human artists, including misled listeners and diverted royalties. Artists can still use AI tools if the final work contains human elements. Tidal has already removed about 66,000 tracks for impersonating artists.
key_points: Tidal will delete 27 million AI-labeled tracks, 6.3 percent of its catalog, on December 9.
43 percent of new uploads in the past 90 days were fully AI-generated, according to Tidal.
Music made with AI tools is still allowed if it contains human elements.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Rackspace shuts down Spot cloud platform after security breach

stories.headline: Rackspace kills Spot cloud platform after Kubernetes breach
stories.dek: Customers have until December 8 to move workloads and data after attackers used stolen credentials to read cluster secrets.
stories.body:
Rackspace is shutting down Rackspace Spot, its Kubernetes container platform, after a breach let attackers access customer clusters and secrets. The service ends permanently on December 8, 2026, at 5 PM Central Time, when remaining workloads will be terminated and data will become inaccessible, according to a customer notice obtained by BleepingComputer.

Attackers got in on November 17 using compromised credentials. They created unauthorized pods, read Kubernetes Secrets and listed nodes and volumes. Rackspace found the intrusion a day later after a customer report and restored service on November 21. The company says Spot is segmented from its core infrastructure and it has found no evidence of wider access.

All Spot customers should treat API tokens, kubeconfigs and Secrets as compromised. On Reddit, some users offered to pay more to keep the service alive.
key_points: Rackspace Spot shuts down December 8, 2026, at 5 PM Central Time; all remaining workloads and data will be lost.
Attackers used compromised credentials on November 17 to create pods and read Kubernetes Secrets in customer clusters.
Rackspace tells all Spot customers to rotate API tokens, refresh tokens, kubeconfigs and Secrets and review logs back to November 16.

sources.name: Ars Technica
sources.title: Microsoft's historic cloud outage exposed an engineering “fog of war”

stories.headline: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after record Exchange Online outage
stories.dek: Internal memos reviewed by Reuters say an urgent fix took up to six days to roll out worldwide, against a one-hour goal.
stories.body:
Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that cut off Exchange Online, Teams and Outlook for users worldwide, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters and reported by Ars Technica. Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson called it the outage with the most customer impact in Exchange Online's history.

In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft's target for its most urgent security fixes is one hour from detection to safe worldwide deployment. "Needless to say, we aren't here yet," he wrote.

Microsoft's November 20 post-incident report blamed an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then added load while maintenance had nearly 14 percent of gateway capacity offline.
key_points: Microsoft declared a "Code Red" engineering overhaul after the November 12 outage, according to memos reviewed by Reuters.
An urgent fix took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation; the goal for top-priority security fixes is one hour.
The company blamed a Windows scalability defect from July, worsened by a Teams failover and nearly 14 percent of gateway capacity offline for maintenance.

opinion.headline: The patch race is lost, so build shields you can switch off
opinion.dek: With AI agents now writing and launching exploits unaided, defenders should fund reversible runtime shields under human approval, not ever faster patch cycles.
opinion.body:
Eleven minutes. That is how long AI agents needed to go from mapping the API of MONAI Label, an open source medical imaging application, to exploiting a previously unknown path traversal flaw in it, BleepingComputer reports, citing Amazon Threat Intelligence. The humans behind the campaign supplied a list of IP addresses and a three-word goal: "obtain shell access." The agents, running on the open source Cairn pentesting framework, did the rest and ended with root on a university server. The campaign ran September 8 to 10. MONAI Label's maintainers shipped a fix on November 18.

Put those dates next to each other and the standard advice, patch faster, looks thin. My argument is that the race to out-patch autonomous attackers is already lost, and that security budgets should move toward temporary, reversible runtime protections that a human approves before they go live. Patching still has to happen. It just cannot be the thing defenders rely on to win on speed.

Start with the offense. Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant found an exposed staging server running a system called exploit_agent, TechRadar reports. It compares code before and after a patch, spots the flaw-related change, writes a working exploit and launches it. In other words, the patch is the map. When the attacker reads the patch faster than the defender can install it, shipping the patch faster is not a strategy. Google counted 11 zero-day exploits per month in 2026, up from at least 8 in 2025, with a peak of 22 in August. Palo Alto Networks tied Cairn to 25 autonomous operations against at least 19 organizations, at least 10 of them breached, according to Ars Technica. Bell Canada says an "agentic" hacker stole enterprise customer data on November 17, BleepingComputer reports.

Now the defense. Microsoft's target for its most urgent security fixes is one hour from detection to safe worldwide deployment, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters and reported by Ars Technica. In a recent incident, an urgent production fix took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. "Needless to say, we aren't here yet," Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson wrote. If Microsoft cannot do it, who can? And the attempt to go faster has costs. Wall Street executives and the NSA told lawmakers that rushed patching caused recent outages, including a flight ground stop, bank lockouts and an NSA network failure, and that no cyberattack was involved, the Washington Sun reports. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has also warned about outdated systems and unpatchable firmware, according to TechRadar. Some things cannot be patched quickly, and some cannot be patched at all.

That is why Shirudo, released this week by OpenAI and Cisco, is the more interesting bet. BleepingComputer and The Hacker News describe it as an open source Linux runtime that uses eBPF to block vulnerable code paths without restarting services. AI agents reproduce an exploit, write a targeted shield and validate it. An operator approves enforcement. Shields ship as signed packages, are verified with TPMs and retire when the real patch lands. OpenAI says a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit against a running Elasticsearch service in a test.

The strongest objection comes from Expel researcher Marcus Hutchins, who told BleepingComputer that letting AI agents write rules affecting the kernel may not be a good idea. He has a point, and there are others. The Elasticsearch result is the vendor's own test. Shirudo is Linux-only. A shield starts from a reproduced exploit, so it would not have stopped the first use of the MONAI Label zero-day. And the attackers are not flawless: Amazon found the campaign because the Cairn instance was left exposed without authentication, and its agents spent 16 hours failing against a Redis server. Google says these frameworks currently "trade stealth for velocity."

None of that rescues the patch race. Google expects more stealth and less human involvement ahead, so today's sloppiness is not a plan. On the kernel worry, compare the two failure modes. A shield is temporary by design, applies without a restart and waits for a human to approve it. A rushed patch pushed across a fleet is the thing banks and the NSA just blamed for outages. I would rather defend a narrow block that an operator signed off on and can retire than a code change shipped in a panic. The human approval step is not a nice extra. It is the whole case for the approach, and buyers should refuse any version that drops it.

What to do with this: anyone self-hosting open source AI applications should assume automated agents are already probing them. Ask vendors what protects a system between disclosure and patch, not only how fast the patch arrives. OpenAI holds a technical webinar on Shirudo on December 15; the thing to watch for is independent testing, not more vendor demos. My prediction is that Microsoft's one-hour goal stays out of reach through its "Code Red" overhaul, and that the gap gets filled by shields, not speed.
opinion.pull_quote: When the attacker reads the patch faster than the defender can install it, shipping the patch faster is not a strategy.
opinion.thesis: Amazon and Google now document AI agents that find, write and launch exploits with no human help, built on open source tools like Cairn, so the race to patch faster is already lost. Rushed patching has caused outages, according to banks and the NSA, and Microsoft took six days to ship an urgent fix. Defenders should invest in reversible runtime shields like Shirudo, with humans approving deployment, rather than in faster patch cycles.
